evidence_for.claim: Cromwell championed liberty of conscience and parliamentary government in rhetoric (e.g., his 1654 speech to the First Protectorate Parliament praising 'liberty of conscience' as a fundamental), yet dissolved multiple parliaments by force when they defied him, most notably the Rump in April 1653 and the First Protectorate Parliament in January 1655.
evidence_for.source: Thomas Carlyle (ed.), 'Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches' (Speech II, 4 September 1654; and account of dissolution of the Rump)

evidence_for.claim: Despite declarations that the Irish campaign was a lawful response and that quarter would be governed by the laws of war, Cromwell ordered the massacre of the Drogheda garrison and many townspeople (September 1649) and sanctioned similar conduct at Wexford, which he then justified in providential religious terms.
evidence_for.source: Cromwell's letter to William Lenthall, Speaker of the Parliament of England, 17 September 1649 (printed in Abbott, 'Writings and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell', vol. II)

evidence_against.claim: Cromwell's professed commitment to religious toleration was substantially honored in practice: he readmitted Jews to England (1656) and generally protected Independents, Baptists, and Quakers from persecution, suggesting consistency between stated principle and action in that domain.
evidence_against.source: Barry Coward, 'Oliver Cromwell' (1991); Whitehall Conference records, December 1655

evidence_for.claim: Cromwell rose to power championing the rights and sovereignty of Parliament against the arbitrary, absolute rule of Charles I, yet he used military force to dissolve the Rump Parliament in 1653 when it defied his wishes, effectively establishing a military dictatorship.

Despite publicly rejecting the title of King in 1657 to maintain the republican facade of the Commonwealth, Cromwell accepted the Humble Petition and Advice, which granted him monarchical powers, a second house of parliament, and the right to name his successor, mirroring the very royal prerogative he had fought to dismantle.
evidence_for.source: Christopher Hill, 'God's Englishman: Oliver Cromwell and the English Revolution'

evidence_against.claim: Cromwell remained remarkably consistent in his core Puritan religious convictions and his belief in 'providence'; his actions, even when politically contradictory, were consistently justified by and aligned with his deeply held, publicly stated belief that he was executing God's will.
evidence_against.source: Antonia Fraser, 'Cromwell: Our Chief of Men'

evidence_for.claim: Publicly stated in speeches that he sought no personal power and fought only for parliamentary rights and godly rule (e.g. 1640s declarations and 1653 dissolution speech), yet dissolved multiple Parliaments by force when they opposed him, ruled via the Instrument of Government with near-monarchical authority, and resided in royal palaces.
evidence_for.source: The Writings and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell, edited by Wilbur Cortez Abbott (Harvard University Press, 1937-1947)

evidence_for.claim: Advocated 'liberty of conscience' for the godly in numerous letters and addresses (e.g. letter to Hammond 1648), yet his regime banned Anglican liturgy, suppressed Catholic worship, and carried out massacres of Irish Catholics at Drogheda and Wexford which he justified in providential terms.
evidence_for.source: Cromwell's Declaration for the Undeceiving of the People of Ireland (1649) and Letters and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell, edited by Thomas Carlyle

evidence_against.claim: Consistently opposed monarchy in line with his stated principles from the Civil War by refusing the crown despite parliamentary pressure and offers in 1657, after months of deliberation citing conscience.
evidence_against.source: The Humble Petition and Advice (1657) and Letters and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell, edited by Thomas Carlyle

evidence_for.claim: Cromwell and the New Model Army publicly justified their cause as the defense of the people's 'just rights and liberties' and denied seeking arbitrary power, yet Cromwell participated in and benefited from military coercion of representative institutions, including Pride's Purge and his armed dissolution of the Rump Parliament in April 1653.
evidence_for.source: A Declaration, or Representation, from His Excellency Sir Thomas Fairfax and the Army under his Command, 14 June 1647, in S. R. Gardiner, ed., The Constitutional Documents of the Puritan Revolution, 1625–1660; Oliver Cromwell, Speech dissolving the Rump Parliament, 20 April 1653, in W. C. Abbott, ed., The Writings and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell

evidence_for.claim: Cromwell repeatedly disclaimed personal ambition and portrayed the army's cause as public rather than self-interested, but he accepted the office of Lord Protector with extensive executive authority, ruled under a written constitution backed by the army, later governed through the Major-Generals, and under the Humble Petition and Advice acquired the power to nominate his successor.
evidence_for.source: The Instrument of Government, 1653, and The Humble Petition and Advice, 1657, in S. R. Gardiner, ed., The Constitutional Documents of the Puritan Revolution, 1625–1660; Austin Woolrych, Britain in Revolution, 1625–1660

evidence_against.claim: The gap was not total: Cromwell did consistently pursue several of his stated priorities, especially Protestant godly reform and a relatively broad, though explicitly limited, liberty of conscience for many Protestant dissenters; he also refused the crown in 1657, which partly aligned with his long-standing suspicion of restored kingship.
evidence_against.source: John Morrill, Oliver Cromwell; The Humble Petition and Advice debates and Cromwell's refusal of the kingship, 1657, in W. C. Abbott, ed., The Writings and Speeches of Oliver Cromwell
